title: Episode 303: Edward III: The Hundred Years' War, the Triumph of Crécy, the Order of the Garter, and the Black Death
description:
The monumental fifty-year reign of King Edward III, who transformed England from a fractured realm into the preeminent military power of Western Europe. Crowned as a teenage puppet in 1327 following the murder of his father, Edward seized power in a midnight coup at Nottingham Castle, executing the usurper Mortimer. Claiming the French throne through his mother Isabella, Edward ignited the Hundred Years' War. With English yeomen longbowmen, he orchestrated the astonishing victory at Crécy, founded the Order of the Garter to resurrect Arthurian chivalric fellowship, and guided his devastated kingdom through the horrors of the Black Death. Discover the chivalric monarch.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series chronicles the sovereign who ruled for half a century, founded the world's most prestigious order of chivalry, and revolutionized European warfare on the blood-soaked slopes of Crécy: King Edward III. Here is George with the grand saga of Edward the Third.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE MIDNIGHT COUP: NOTTINGHAM CASTLE: 1327 TO 1330
When fourteen-year-old Edward III was crowned at Westminster in February 1327, he was king in name alone. Real power was wielded with tyrannical arrogance by his mother Queen Isabella and her ambitious lover, Roger Mortimer, who kept the boy king under watchful guard while squandering royal revenues and signing a humiliating peace treaty with Scotland. Young Edward chafed in bitter silence, nursing a burning resolve to reclaim his royal birthright and avenge the horrific, mysterious murder of his father Edward II. In October 1330, the royal court gathered at Nottingham Castle for a Great Council. Mortimer, suspecting conspiracy, demanded the castle keys each night and surrounded himself with armed retainers. But the loyal castle constable, Sir William Montagu, revealed to Edward a secret subterranean passage carved deep into the sandstone rock, known to this day as Mortimer's Hole. Under cover of absolute midnight darkness, Edward and a dozen trusted companions crept through the damp labyrinth, burst into Mortimer's bedchamber, and overpowered his guards after a fierce, echoing swordfight. Despite Queen Isabella's desperate cries from the doorway—'Fair son, fair son, have pity on gentle Mortimer!'—Edward was unyielding. Mortimer was dragged to London and hanged at Tyburn as a traitor. At eighteen years of age, Edward III announced to Europe that he would govern his kingdom by his own hand and royal will alone. The underground sally port, carved through the sandstone cliffs above the River Leen, had been kept secret even from the queen's chief stewards. When Edward's men broke into the bedchamber, they found Mortimer desperately trying to reach his sword, but he was pinned to the floor by Montagu's knights. Edward personally escorted his mother Isabella to Castle Rising in Norfolk, treating her with royal dignity and an annual pension, but permanently stripping her of political authority.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: CLAIMING THE CROWN OF FRANCE: THE OUTBREAK OF THE HUNDRED YEARS' WAR
Determined to restore the martial prestige of the English crown, Edward first campaigned aggressively against Scotland, avenging the defeat of Bannockburn at Halidon Hill in 1333, where massed English archers decimated the charging Scottish pike schiltrons. But a far greater destiny beckoned across the English Channel. When the direct line of the French House of Capet died out in 1328, Edward was the closest living male relative of the late French king, being the son of Isabella of France. The French nobility, invoking what they termed Salic Law to bar succession through female lineage, crowned Philip of Valois as King Philip VI. In 1337, when Philip confiscated Edward's ancestral duchy of Gascony, Edward responded with breathtaking audacity: he formally assumed the title and arms of King of France, quartering the English golden lions with the French blue fleur-de-lis on his royal banner. Thus began the titanic struggle known to history as the Hundred Years' War. In 1340, at the naval Battle of Sluys off the coast of Flanders, Edward commanded his fleet in person, maneuvering his ships with the wind and sun behind them to unleash clouds of armor-piercing bodkin arrows upon the tightly packed French armada. The French fleet was annihilated, securing total English mastery of the Channel and opening the path for a full-scale invasion of continental France. At the Battle of Sluys, the collision of warships was so ferocious and deafening that English chroniclers described the sound as an earthquake on water. The French ships, chained together in four defensive lines, became deathtraps under the raining bodkin arrowheads; over eighteen thousand French sailors and knights were slain or drowned, leaving King Philip's jester to famously break the news to the French court by remarking that English sailors had no stomach to jump into the sea as the brave French had.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ENGLISH LONGBOW AT CRÉCY: AUGUST 26, 1346
In July 1346, Edward landed in Normandy with fifteen thousand men, marching across northern France in a lightning chevauchée that ravaged the countryside and pushed to the very outskirts of Paris. Cornered near the village of Crécy by a French royal army numbering over thirty thousand, including the elite heavy cavalry of European Christendom and six thousand Genoese mercenary crossbowmen, Edward chose his ground with consummate genius. He dismounted his knights, dug defensive ditches, and positioned thousands of Welsh and English longbowmen in a harrow formation along the terraced hillside of the Vallée des Clercs. When the French king ordered an impetuous charge in late afternoon, a sudden summer thunderstorm soaked the crossbow strings of the Genoese, rendering them useless, while English archers kept their bows dry inside waxed canvas sleeves. As the sun broke through behind the English lines, blinding the French, the yeomen unleashed an apocalyptic storm of steel. Drawing six-foot war bows of seasoned yew with draw weights exceeding one hundred and twenty pounds, English archers fired ten to twelve arrows a minute. The sky darkened as tens of thousands of arrows fell like lethal hail. French cavalry charged again and again, sixteen times into the teeth of the gale, only to have their warhorses butchered and noble knights impaled in muddy piles. Edward's sixteen-year-old son, the Black Prince, commanded the right wing, winning his chivalric spurs in blood. Crécy was a slaughter that shattered French feudal power. The English longbowmen were seasoned veterans from the Welsh Marches and English shires, men whose left arms were deformed by bone spurs from a lifetime of pulling monstrous bows. Edward positioned his royal command post at a stone windmill high above the battlefield, from which he could overlook the entire slaughter. When messengers arrived pleading for reinforcements for the Black Prince's beleaguered division, Edward calmly responded: 'Let the boy win his spurs, for I will that the day be his, and that the honor of it be his.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: CHIVALRY AND ARTHURIAN FELLOWSHIP: THE ORDER OF THE GARTER: 1348
Following the triumph of Crécy and the grueling eleven-month siege and capture of the vital port of Calais, King Edward returned to England as the undisputed paragon of European chivalry. He was deeply captivated by the legends of King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table, even commissioning a vast circular stone building at Windsor Castle where two hundred knights could feast as equals. In 1348, Edward distilled this romantic Arthurian dream into the founding of the Most Noble Order of the Garter, the oldest and highest order of chivalry in Great Britain. According to court tradition, while the king was dancing at a grand victory banquet with the Countess of Salisbury, her blue silk garter slipped from her leg and fell to the floor, prompting muffled snickers and whispers among the gathered courtiers. King Edward stepped forward, gallantly picked up the garter, and tied it around his own leg, exclaiming in Anglo-Norman French: 'Honi soit qui mal y pense'—'Shame on him who thinks evil of it!' Adding: 'Shortly shall they see that garter held in such high honor that they will be proud to wear it.' The Order was limited to the sovereign and twenty-five companion knights, uniting the realm's fiercest battlefield commanders in an unbreakable bond of loyalty to the Crown, with St. George's Chapel at Windsor as their sacred spiritual sanctuary. Edward had elevated medieval warfare into a sacred fraternity of king and aristocracy. To further dignify his Arthurian order, Edward established twenty-six 'Poor Knights' of Windsor—later known as the Military Knights of Windsor—veteran soldiers who had fallen on hard times, who were housed at the castle to pray daily for the Sovereign and Companions of the Garter. The annual Garter Day procession on St. George's Day, with its flowing mantles of deep blue velvet, embroidered badges, and gold collars of interlocking knots, became the most celebrated spectacle of courtly majesty in fourteenth-century Europe.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BLACK DEATH: THE PLAGUE THAT RESHAPED ENGLAND: 1348 TO 1350
At the height of Edward's military glory, an invisible, apocalyptic catastrophe struck the kingdom. In the summer of 1348, a merchant ship from Gascony docked at Weymouth in Dorset, carrying infected black rats and fleas harboring Yersinia pestis: the Black Death. Within weeks, the virulent pestilence swept through towns and villages with terrifying, unstoppable fury. Victims developed swollen, agonizing buboes in the groin and armpits, coughed black blood, and perished within three days of falling ill. The royal family itself was not spared: Edward's beloved fourteen-year-old daughter, Princess Joan, traveling to Spain to marry the heir of Castile, contracted the plague in Bordeaux and died in agony. Between a third and a half of the entire population of England perished in less than eighteen months. Entire villages were abandoned, fields lay unharvested with rotting crops, and the dead were dumped into mass burial pits outside London's city walls. The catastrophic loss of labor shattered the ancient feudal system: surviving serfs demanded higher wages and freedom of movement, leading Edward's parliament to pass the controversial Ordinance of Labourers in 1349 to freeze wages. The social order of medieval England was irrevocably transformed, setting the stage for future peasant uprisings. The psychological trauma of the Black Death shook medieval English religious and social certainty to its very foundation. Parish priests fled their churches rather than administer the last rites, leaving corpses to decompose in houses until neighbors boarded up the doors. When the pestilence finally subsided, the acute shortage of agricultural laborers empowered serfs to demand cash wages, shattering manorial bonds and fostering an independent, prosperous yeoman class that would forever change the English countryside.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TREATY OF BRÉTIGNY AND THE TWILIGHT YEARS: 1360 TO 1377
Despite the ravages of the plague, English arms continued to triumph abroad under Edward's gifted warrior sons. In 1356, the Black Prince won a stunning victory at Poitiers, capturing King John II of France himself. In 1360, Edward concluded the Treaty of Brétigny, securing full sovereign control over a vast Angevin realm comprising Aquitaine, Gascony, Poitou, and Calais, without paying homage to the French king, in exchange for temporarily renouncing his claim to the French crown. But the final decade of Edward's reign was clouded by sorrow, physical decline, and the painful unraveling of his conquests. The new French king, Charles V, adopted a cautious strategy of attrition and Fabian warfare, avoiding pitched battles while slowly recapturing English fortresses. Back in England, Edward's beloved queen, Philippa of Hainault, died in 1369, leaving the aging king heartbroken. Plagued by illness and early dementia, Edward fell completely under the sway of his greedy and manipulative mistress, Alice Perrers, who openly enriched herself at the expense of the royal treasury and wore the late queen's jewels at public tournaments, provoking widespread outrage among the English nobility and common people alike. The capture of King John II at Poitiers allowed Edward to demand a king's ransom of three million gold écus, equivalent to twice the annual revenue of England. Yet the burden of maintaining foreign garrisons across vast French territories ignited relentless fiscal deficits at home. As the aging monarch withdrew into grief following Queen Philippa's passing, Alice Perrers sat openly upon the King's Bench in Westminster, intimidating judges and meddling in royal pardons, a scandal that thoroughly tarnished the sunset of Edward's heroic reign.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE GOOD PARLIAMENT AND THE LEGACY OF EDWARD III
In 1376, popular fury boiled over in what became known as the Good Parliament. In a revolutionary constitutional moment, the House of Commons exercised the power of parliamentary impeachment for the first time in English history, removing corrupt royal ministers and banishing Alice Perrers from court. Tragedy struck the royal family in June 1376 when the Black Prince died of chronic dysentery at age forty-five, leaving his ten-year-old son, Richard of Bordeaux, as heir to the throne. On June 21, 1377, King Edward III died at Sheen Palace at the age of sixty-four, abandoned by his courtiers, with legend recounting that Alice Perrers stripped the gold rings from his dying fingers before fleeing the bedchamber. Edward III had reigned for fifty years, five months, and twenty-eight days. He had forged the English Parliament into an indispensable institution with two distinct chambers, established English as the official language of the royal courts and parliament in place of French, and instilled an enduring national identity of pride and martial prowess. Buried beside Queen Philippa in Westminster Abbey beneath a magnificent gilt-bronze effigy, Edward III stood as the grandest monument to England's high medieval chivalric age. Edward's reign permanently reshaped English governance: by requiring Parliament's assent for taxation, he elevated the Commons from humble petitioning burgesses into indispensable partners in government. He established the Office of Justice of the Peace in every English county, decentralizing local justice, and declared the Statute of Treasons in 1352, codifying high treason for centuries. When he was laid to rest at Westminster Abbey, the realm mourned not just a conqueror, but the father of an emergent, united English nation.
